Description: The Digital Object Identifier (DOI) for the resource. It is a persistent identifier used to uniquely identify objects.
The prefix part of the DOI, assigned by a registration agency. This field is used when minting a new DOI.
The suffix part of the DOI, chosen by the client to uniquely identify the resource. This field is used when minting a new DOI.
The event state of the DOI, such as 'draft', 'registered', or 'findable'. It determines the DOI's publication status.
The URL of the landing page for the resource that the DOI resolves to. This is a mandatory field for making a DOI findable.
Information about the type of the resource. It includes a general type from a controlled list (e.g., Software, Dataset) and an optional free-text description.
The main researchers or authors involved in producing the resource, in priority order. Each creator can be a person or an organization.
The names or titles by which the resource is known. At least one main title is required.
The name of the entity that holds, archives, publishes, or otherwise distributes the resource. This is typically an organization.
The year when the resource was or will be made publicly available. This must be a four-digit year.
Subjects, keywords, classification codes, or key phrases describing the resource. This helps with discoverability.
Institutions or persons responsible for collecting, managing, or otherwise contributing to the resource. Each contributor has a specific role.
Different dates relevant to the resource, such as creation, publication, or update dates. Each date entry must have a type indicating its meaning.
The primary language of the resource, specified using an IETF BCP 47 language tag.
Any other identifiers for the resource, such as a local identifier or a URL to a code repository.
Identifiers of related resources, along with the nature of the relationship (e.g., 'IsPartOf', 'HasVersion', 'Cites').
Information about related resources that are not identified by a formal persistent identifier. This can include descriptive text about the related item.
Unstructured size information about the resource, such as '15 MiB' or '100 pages'.
Technical format of the resource, preferably using IANA media types like 'application/json' or 'text/csv'.
The version number of the resource. It is recommended to use semantic versioning where appropriate.
Information about rights held in and over the resource, such as a license. It is recommended to use an SPDX license identifier and URI.
Different descriptions for the resource, such as an abstract or table of contents. Each description must have a type indicating its nature.
Spatial regions or named places where the data was collected or is about. Can be a point, a bounding box, or a polygon.
Information about financial support (funding) for the resource. This includes the funder name, award information, and funder identifier.
The URI of the DataCite metadata schema used. For this model, the value is fixed to the DataCite Kernel v4 schema URL.
Information about the larger resource that contains this resource, such as a journal or a book series. This property helps create parent-child relationships.
